In traditional making the tube is hollowed out of a solid piece of bamboo or of animal bone, which gives good acoustic properties. Clay three-hole pipes are shaped from clay and fired, and have a warm timbre. Modern versions often use hard woods such as paulownia or cypress for the tube, which keeps them durable and the tone stable. The edges of the holes are sometimes polished, while the inside of the instrument is usually left rough or lightly sanded to keep the traditional character of the sound.

The basic method is to hold the pipe in one hand, blow to sound it, and open and close the three fingerholes to change pitch; the other hand stays free and can at the same time strike a tabor drum, bell, psaltery, string drum, clappers or triangle. Beginners first practise holding the pipe steadily in one hand and opening and closing the holes, then add the rhythm of the other hand. The interval layout differs from region to region — whole tone, semitone, whole tone, or whole tone, whole tone, semitone — and has to follow the type of pipe you are using.

It is usually played with one hand while the other strikes a small drum, bell, psaltery, string drum, clappers or triangle. In the Basque Country it provides the music for traditional dance ensembles together with the small drum; in Andalusia it is used at festivals, the May Cross, sword dances and pilgrimage celebrations, and at the Romería del Rocío in Huelva it is called the pilgrimage flute or the higher-pitched whistle flute.

In the Basque Country its standing rose over the last century, and especially after the end of the Franco regime it became a mark of Basque identity and folk culture, with local pipe-and-drum schools accompanying traditional dance groups. In Andalusia it is used at celebrations, the May Cross festival, sword dances and pilgrimage processions; around El Rocío in Huelva it is called the rociera flute, or the higher-pitched rociera whistle. Provence, the Basque Country and England commonly use different note sequences; England uses whole tone, whole tone, semitone, matching the lowest three holes of the tin whistle.

Its range is comparatively limited, usually spanning one or two octaves, and the pitch depends on which combinations of holes are open. Because the structure is simple the resonating space is limited, and the volume is moderate but carrying, with a warm nasal resonance.

The three-hole pipe (tabor pipe, galoubet) is an aerophone built on three holes and designed to be played with one hand while the other plays a tabor drum, bell, psalterium, tambourin à cordes, bone plates, triangle or other percussion. Its origin is unknown; it can be traced back at least to the twelfth century, and it was long widespread in France, the Iberian Peninsula and England and is still in use today. In the Basque Country, over the past century and especially after the final years of the Franco regime, it became a mark of identity and folk culture, and new pipe-and-drum schools accompany traditional dance ensembles with the tabor drum. In Andalusia it is used at celebrations, the May Cross festival, sword dances and pilgrimage festivals; at the El Rocío pilgrimage it is also called flauta rociera and similar names.

Its tone combines a folk character with a plain elegance, and it suits folk song and pastoral scenes especially well. Because breath control shapes the timbre so strongly, the player's breathing technique directly determines the warmth and steadiness of the tone, which gives the instrument a highly individual expressive character.
